  pale-yellow layer.
- **Film thickness.** "Very, very fine layers"; a "gossamer-thin
  film".
- **Pooling.** The thin paint "accumulated in the depths of the textured
  ground layers," producing the finest dots of color and "almost
  continuous gradations" without visible brushstrokes.
- **Stippling.** Some passages are stippled, which "enhance[s] the
  transparency and light scattering".
- **Strokes.** Early brushwork is "painstaking… small strokes of paint
  placed side by side like a closely woven textile". Paint
  was modeled while still wet.
- **Impasto.** Limited in early works; some later works mix thick
  and thin paint and leave the ground bare in places.
- **Order of work.** Ground (bought), then underdrawing, then a "very thin
  underpainting," then paint; small details were added last,
  over finished passages.

## 7. Condition and aging

- **Fragility.** The thin paint made the paintings "exceptionally prone to
  damage"; many micro-losses come from abrasion in past
  cleaning.
- **Smalt discoloration.** Smalt has partly lost its color in one painting:
  low potassium (4.9 wt%) and changed cobalt coordination show an
  intermediate stage of degradation; a simulation of the original colors
  comes out cooler and bluer. Smalt can turn brown over
  time.
- **Craquelure.** One painting has an elongated craquelure, probably from
  pressure on the back.
- **Pentimenti.** Few.

## 8. Greens

- **Mostly mixed.** The Dresden team (14 paintings) writes that "the
  palette was very sparing" but the greens show a "lush variety"
  ("üppige Vielfalt"). The true greens were "copper-containing pigments
  and green earth." Greens were often mixed from blue and yellow: Prussian
  blue "very often," smalt and cobalt blue as well, with yellow ocher,
  Naples yellow or chrome yellow. Green passages often have
  "several (up to four) layers of different greens".
- **One painting of 1808.** Copper and arsenic were found in the same
  green layer of *Bohemian Landscape with Mount Milešovka*. The Dresden
  researchers interpret this as a degraded copper-arsenic green.
- **Rinmann's green**, rare, found on three paintings of about 1819–23.
- **A dating test.** A painting was de-attributed partly because its greens
  are cobalt blue mixed with chrome yellow, anachronistic for its supposed
  date of 1798/99.

| Green | Date and availability |
| --- | --- |
| Green earth (terre verte) | Ancient; in painters' manuals through the 19th century |
| Verdigris / copper resinate | Old; "rarely found in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century paintings"; around 1816 still made as green "varnishes" |
| Scheele's green (copper arsenite) | "Introduced in 1778"; "use as an artist's pigment is little documented" |
| Schweinfurt/emerald green | Made from 1814; a trade secret until 1822; sold in tubes from 1832; earliest easel finds c.1832 |
| Rinmann's green (cobalt-zinc oxide) | 1780; "poor tinting strength and high cost… kept it in limited use" |
| Chromium oxide (opaque) | "Rarely used because of its high price" (1831); earliest finds 1845–50 |
| Viridian | Made c.1838, patented 1859, earliest finds 1863 |
| Chrome green (chrome yellow + Prussian blue) | Appeared shortly after chrome yellow; chrome yellow made commercially in Germany only from 1820 |

Green earth is translucent, weak and short of body.

## 9. The tubes here

The supplied box contains lead white, smalt, pale smalt, yellow ochre,
red earth, vermilion, raw umber, bone black, cobalt blue, chrome yellow,
Prussian blue, green earth, Rinmann's green, copper green, Naples yellow
and rose madder: a selection
from materials documented across Friedrich's career. Ochers and yellow
earths correspond to yellow ochre; red earths and red iron oxide to red
earth; cinnabar to vermilion. The supplied copper green is verdigris
ground in oil.

Naples yellow is lead antimonate. The supplied red lake is rose madder,
a madder lake on alumina. The easel guide lists each tube's
properties.

## 10. At this easel

- **Support.** Plain-weave linen with layered grounds laid from the tubes.
  Knife application levels the weave; roller and brush application leave
  their own fine texture. The preparation is dry when painting starts.
- **Drawing.** Graphite pencils, black chalk and ruled lines.
- **Paint.** Tube mixtures can be ground in linseed, walnut or poppy oil.
  Added oil makes a mixture more transparent and fluid. `turps=` thins it
  with solvent that evaporates as the paint is laid; `thinner=` leaves
  solvent in the film to evaporate over painting time. The guide describes
  both methods.
- **Taking paint off.** Brushes pick up wet paint as they pass. A rag
  wipes or blots wet paint; a painting knife scrapes it with its blade.
- **Everything else** the easel does is in the easel guide.

# Physics of oil paint on canvas

**Tags.** **[V]**: the number is in the source text. **[S]**: the number is from a summary of the source. **[E]**: an estimate or derivation, with its assumptions stated.

---

## 1. Rheology and leveling

**Constitutive behavior.** Tube oil paint is a viscoplastic, shear-thinning and thixotropic suspension. A Herschel–Bulkley law fits it well: τ = τ_y + K·γ̇ⁿ, with n ≈ 0.2–0.7[S].

| Quantity | Value | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Yield stress, model ultramarine oil paint (32 vol% solids) | **10–20 Pa**. Brushstrokes came out regular and low-relief (Rz < 100 µm) | [V] |
| Yield stress, same paint + 4 vol% egg yolk (capillary network) | **≈3000–3200 Pa**. Strong impasto, and wrinkling suppressed | [V] |
| Typical tube paints | ~10–1000 Pa; stiff impasto grades above 1000 Pa | [S] |
| Apparent viscosity | 10⁴–10⁷ Pa·s at 0.01–0.1 s⁻¹; 10–10³ Pa·s at 10–100 s⁻¹ (brushing) | [S] |
| Linseed oil (the medium) | η ≈ 0.048 Pa·s, σ ≈ 33–36 mN/m at 20 °C | [S] |
| Stand oil | η ≈ 0.5–25 Pa·s depending on grade | [S] |

Impasto requires "sufficiently high yield stress preventing levelling after brush passage," while brushability depends on the *high-shear* viscosity, so stiff paint can still brush easily[V].

**Orchard leveling (Newtonian, thin film h ≪ λ).** A sinusoidal ridge of wavelength λ on a film of mean thickness h decays as a(t) = a₀·e^(−t/τ), with

  **τ = 3η(λ/2π)⁴ / (σh³)**[V].

The dependence is λ⁴ and h⁻³, so λ and h matter far more than η or σ.

**Yield-stress floor.** Surface tension produces a leveling stress of about 8π³σha/λ³. Flow stops once τ_y exceeds it, so ridges smaller than

  **a_c = τ_y λ³ / (8π³ σ h)**

stay frozen[S]. For thixotropic paint, τ_y(t) recovers after brushing, so leveling starts and then freezes with a residual mark[S]. With solvent evaporation, moderate yield stress can reduce residual unevenness[S].

**Worked numbers [E]** (σ = 0.035 N/m):

| Case | η | λ | h | τ (1/e time) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Medium-rich glaze, bristle striation | 1 Pa·s | 0.3 mm | 20 µm | 0.06 s |
| Glaze, stroke-scale ridge | 1 Pa·s | 2 mm | 20 µm | 110 s |
| Tube paint, stroke ridge, low-shear η | 10³–10⁴ Pa·s | 2 mm | 100 µm | 15 min – 2.5 h |

| τ_y | Frozen amplitude a_c, λ = 0.3 mm, h = 100 µm | a_c, λ = 2 mm, h = 300 µm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 15 Pa | ~0.5–1 µm | ~45 µm |
| 100 Pa | ~3–6 µm | ~300 µm |
| 500 Pa | ~15–30 µm | effectively frozen |
| 3000 Pa | ~90–200 µm | frozen |

The ranges come from comparing the thin-film form with a deep-layer form, a_c ≈ τ_yλ²/(4π²σ), derived for h ≳ λ/2π, where the lubrication assumption fails [E]. **Inferred for this case:** at the example's λ = 0.3 mm and h = 100 µm, the estimated arrest amplitude rises from about 0.5–1 µm at 15 Pa to about 3–6 µm at 100 Pa. Retained relief depends on wavelength, thickness, initial amplitude and recovering rheology, so no single yield stress marks where striations become visible. The Newtonian glaze example predicts that fine striations level quickly. Which marks stay visible also depends on conditions these calculations leave out.

## 2. Brush marks

| Fiber | Diameter | Tip | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hog bristle | 0.20–0.30 mm (fine hog 0.15–0.25) | Naturally split ("flagged") | [S] |
| Kolinsky/red sable | ~60–120 µm | Single fine taper | [S] |

In profilometry of oil paintings, the height features that best identify the painter sit at **0.2–0.4 mm**, matching the bristle widths used (**0.25 and 0.65 mm**)[V]. For macro impasto, a 17th-century canvas has measured relief up to about 0.85 mm[S].

**Dry brush and scumble.** A technical description of an 1879/80 canvas reports "an almost dry brush [dragged] across the surface, catching only the thread tops". This works even over a heavy, smooth ground: the paint goes where the brush touches.

## 3. Film formation and drying

- **Mass and skin timeline.** A titanium white in alkali-refined linseed oil (10 mil ≈ 250 µm film) gained nearly **16%** of its oil weight in the first days. It "begins to skin over" as it nears the peak and is touch-dry at **4–6 days**. Cold-pressed and alkali-refined oils peak at **15–18%** and then slowly lose mass over a year or more[V].
- **Thickness.** Thicker oil-paint films generally take longer to dry. Drying also depends on pigment, oil and additives. The easel guide describes drying in this studio.
- **Induction.** Drying oils take up oxygen only after an induction period; driers shorten it or speed the uptake. Lead white alone barely speeds the oxidation of linseed oil, and its impurities (litharge, lead acetate) probably account for its reputation as a drier[S].
- **Skinning and wrinkling.** Oxygen enters through the surface, so a crosslinked skin forms over mobile paint. Wrinkling is a compressive buckle of that skin. It is worse in thick, oil-rich or drier-heavy films[V]. Raising τ_y to about 3200 Pa suppressed wrinkling in model paints[V].
- **Long-term shrinkage and brittleness** (films 21–31 years old, cold-pressed linseed oil)[S]:

| Paint | Cumulative shrinkage | Aged strain at break | Aged modulus |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lead white | 0.5% | 0.3–0.8% | ~1 GPa |
| Lead white + litharge | 0.9% | 0.5% | ~2.9 GPa |
| Zinc white | 0.3% | 0.1–0.3% | 2–3 GPa |
| Verdigris | 1.7% | 0.1% | — |
| Red iron oxide | ~0% | 0.3% | ~50 MPa |

  Lead white's strain at break fell from **7.3% at 0.2 years** to under 1% at 31 years[S]. Chalk-glue grounds are modeled with a break strain of **0.002**[V].
- **Layer thicknesses.** A three-layer commercial ground from about 1880 measured **1.5–30 µm (chalk), 5–35 µm and 10–45 µm (lead white)**[V]. Mock-up oil layers measured **59–125 µm for one coat** and 110–188 µm for two[S]. Single paint layers run roughly 10–200+ µm [S; general cross-section ranges, low confidence].
- **Conformal or filling.** That ground is "thicker and smoother, greatly diminishing the texture of the canvas weave"[V]. In the Newtonian free-surface model, thinner films level more slowly at fixed viscosity and wavelength, because τ ∝ h⁻³. At η = 1 Pa·s and σ = 0.035 N/m, λ = 0.3–0.8 mm and h = 10–20 µm give 1/e times of about 0.056–22.5 seconds, which can be fast compared with drying. Whether weave relief survives depends on viscosity, yield stress, contact during application and drying, as well as on film thickness[E].

## 4. Canvas and ground

**Thread counts (plain weave unless noted).** These are measurements of individual paintings, not period averages.

| Canvas | Threads/cm | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| French 18th-century hemp | mostly 12–14 × 9.5–13 | [V] |
| French 18th century, hemp warp and linen weft | 17 × 14 | [V] |
| French 19th century | 10 × 6 (coarse) to 16 × 10 | [V] |
| Twill linen, 1830 | 30 × 29 | [V] |
| Fine linen, 1855 | 38 × 34 | [V] |
| Commercial canvas, 1879/80 | 26.0 × 29.9 | [V] |
| Commercial roll (Tasset et L'Hôte), 1888–90 | ~12 × 15–17 (e.g., 12.3 × 17.3) | [S] |

A usable range for 19th-century canvases is **10–38 threads/cm**, which is a **0.26–1.0 mm pitch**. Warp and weft often differ by 10–40%.

- **Irregularity.** Density along the warp is always more consistent than along the weft[V]. Weft "slubs" (thick spots) are the usual irregularity[S].
- **Cusping (scalloping).** This is "a regular scalloping of the threads at the perimeter" left by the tacks used while the canvas was sized and grounded[V]. On the 1879/80 canvas the original tacks were **5.5–6 cm apart**[V]. Commercial pre-primed rolls often show *no* cusping on edges cut from the roll[V].
- **Ground and texture.** Late-19th-century commercial grounds were either *à grain* (one layer, so more weave texture shows) or *lisse* (two layers, fills the interstices)[S]. An **estimate is 5–40 µm** peak to valley under *à grain* and about 2–10 µm under *lisse* **[E, unverified]**.
- **Mechanics.** Above about 80% RH the canvas *shrinks* as crimp increases, and once dry the glue size, not the canvas, carries the tension[V].

content.thinking:
I'm drawing on Friedrich's recurring motifs—rückenfigur, moonrise, ruins, fog—to imagine my own scene: a twilight moonrise over a still Baltic shore with two figures on rocks beneath a sky shifting from salmon to deeper hues.

Settling on the composition: "Evening on the Bodden" — a dark foreground spit with dolmen-like boulders, a solitary figure gazing over a still lagoon toward a distant shore, under a luminous sunset sky grading from yellow to green-gray to blue-violet, with a crescent moon, evening star, and maybe a few bare trees, echoing Friedrich's low-horizon, symmetrical compositions.

I'm planning the layout in detail: landscape format around 700mm wide, sky filling the top 62% with a warm horizon glow grading into cool blues toward the top, a crescent moon and star placed upper-right, a thin bluish headland on the left possibly with a tiny spire, still water reflecting the glow with a horizontal light streak, and a dark foreground shoreline of stones and grass.

Rising from that foreground I'm picturing a rocky knoll with one or two Rückenfigur figures silhouetted against the bright water, plus distant sailboats as small dark shapes and a few large boulders catching cool rim light in front. I realize this is essentially Friedrich's "Moonrise over the Sea," so since the brief calls for an original composition, I'm considering alternatives -- a frozen lagoon, a winter dusk with a bare oak and hunter, or some other scene that isn't just a direct restaging.

I try "Fisherman's Cross at Dusk," with a weathered wooden cross and net on a dune, a woman seated on an overturned boat watching the afterglow -- but the cross-by-the-sea motif overlaps too closely with Friedrich's "Cross on the Baltic." I keep searching for something more singular, toying with ideas like paired anchors or a vertical mountain scene with morning mist.

Then another option comes to mind: a lone figure with a staff on an Elbe sandstone plateau, leaning pine beside them, looking out over a mist-filled valley where distant ridges emerge in paler blue-gray layers under a rising moon in a peach sky -- Friedrich-like but freshly arranged. Weighing the two, I decide the layered mist valley offers a richer depth problem than a single sea gradient, so I commit to the moonrise mist valley in landscape format and start planning the composition dimensions.

I'm working out the sky gradient from cool dark blue at the top down to a warm pale glow near the horizon, placing a small pale moon just above the farthest ridge slightly right of center, and positioning the Rückenfigur on the foreground rock to the left so it gazes toward the rising moon.

For the layered landscape, I'm planning several ridges of mountain silhouettes growing darker and bluer toward the viewer with soft mist bands at their feet, a mid-ground forested ridge of spruce tops emerging from the mist, and a dark foreground outcrop with fir trees, a dead trunk, and warm umber-green tones catching the moon's glow.

I'm thinking about the twilight palette now—a warm moonrise glow against a sky that could show the pink Belt of Venus above a blue-gray earth shadow near the horizon, settling on a working palette of lead white, smalt, Prussian blue, yellow ochre, Naples yellow, red earth, rose madder, raw umber, bone black, and green earth.

For the canvas construction, I'm following Friedrich's method: fine linen, a lower red-ochre ground applied by knife, then a lighter lead white layer brushed thin enough that the striations show through, deciding on a brushed rather than rolled application to get that textured effect in the sky.

For scale, at 700mm wide with 14 threads/cm, one unit roughly matches the thread pitch so the weave reads correctly at this size. I'm planning the underdrawing in graphite, followed by thin turpentine underpainting, then one or two thin layers with stippling for gradations, saving details for last.

I should check a few reference techniques for rocks and tree structure, particularly how spruces are typically rendered.

{"id": "oil-blending", "title": "Blending at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Blending

- **Blend inside one passage.** Shape the mask like the passage, with its
  edge where the paint already matches. Keep everything you want to keep
  outside the mask, dry shapes included: the blender carries wet paint onto
  them.
- **Look after each pass.** The blender lifts paint as it moves it. When
  darks go pale, texture flattens or the weave shows through, stop.
- **A seam that keeps coming back** needs another method. A smaller patch
  blended again rebuilds the box. Try something else across the whole
  transition on the scratch canvas: a thin tint of the original recipe,
  interlocking strokes of the two neighboring colors over dry paint, or the
  connected passage repainted up to its natural edges.
"}

{"id": "oil-ground", "title": "Oil ground handling at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Ground

- An **oil ground** (the default) absorbs nothing: paint stays open and
  glossy longer. An **absorbent ground** (`absorbent=true`) drinks the oil of
  thin paint: matte, lean, quick to set, colors that sit on the surface;
  thick paint is barely touched. Choose before you start: it is the
  canvas's character.
- A **toned ground** (a little ochre, umber or black in the white) sets the
  middle value from the first stroke; a white ground keeps everything high
  in key and lets thin paint glow.
"}

  foreground boulders with the knife "almost like relief sculptures". In a grotto picture he "laid it on, scraped it off,
  laying and scraping over and over again" to get a marbled effect, and

{"id": "tree-structure", "title": "Tree structure and species", "page": 1, "pages": 4, "next_page": 2, "text": "# Trees: how they are built

*A note on how trees grow, branch and taper, from documented sources. "General knowledge" marks statements not tied to a source; "My inference" marks conclusions drawn from sourced facts.*

## In short

1. **A tree is a branching system that grows at its tips and thickens everywhere.** Strong side branches arise mostly near the top of each year's shoot (acrotony). Upright axes build the frame; side axes spread sideways. When a tip dies, the one or more side shoots below it take over, so the axis forks or zigzags.
2. **Diameter is conserved across forks, roughly.** The cross-section below a fork about equals the sum of the cross-sections above it (the branch-area rule). The measured exponent is 1.8–2.3 instead of exactly 2. Every twig is the thin end of a continuous path to the roots.
3. **A side branch is thickest where it leaves its parent.** It is set into the trunk as a sleeve: the branch's own wood turns down and wraps its base as a collar, and trunk wood wraps over that collar every year. A swelling underneath (the branch collar) and usually a raised ridge of bark on top (the branch bark ridge) mark the junction.
4. **Healthy crowns end in a network of long shoots; stressed ones don't.** Roloff's four vitality stages run from a net of long shoots at the crown edge (healthy) to spiky "bottle-brush" tips, then bushy chains of short shoots, then dieback and a shrinking crown.

**Terms used below.** *Acrotony*: side branches strongest near the tip of the parent shoot. *Orthotropic/plagiotropic*: growing upright/growing sideways. *Long shoot/short shoot*: a year's extension that is long and carries branches versus a stubby one. *Epicormic shoot*: a shoot from a dormant bud on an old trunk or limb (German *Wasserreiser*). *Reiteration*: the tree repeating its own basic architecture as a new sub-crown. *Retrenchment*: natural shrinking of an old crown. *Cladoptosis*: a tree's regular shedding of twigs at an abscission layer. *Sapwood/heartwood*: conducting outer wood/non-conducting inner wood.

## 1. How a tree is built

- **Growth rules.** Branches that develop mostly in the distal part of a parent shoot (acrotony) are what give a tree its tree-like rather than bushy habit. Upright (orthotropic) axes "are generally associated with plant skeleton construction." Sideways (plagiotropic) axes explore horizontal space and carry leaves and flowers. If a shoot's tip dies, aborts or turns into a flower, one, two or more branches take over below it (sympodial branching). A string of such takeovers can still look like one straight axis.
- **Limbs, branches, twigs.** Branches carry branches, and those carry twigs; in sympodial trees the steps pile up quickly. **General knowledge:** a mature broadleaved crown commonly has five or more such steps from trunk to this year's twig; I found no source that counts them species by species. Seen from any distance, only the trunk and the first limbs or two read as separate shapes; the finer branching merges into the crown's texture and the ragged edge of its outline.
- **Crowns within the crown.** As a crown matures, big limbs grow crowns of their own, each shaped by where it sits in the tree; this "sequential" reiteration is a normal part of crown construction. After damage, dormant buds produce "traumatic" reiteration: new small crowns on the wounded frame. **General knowledge:** an old crown therefore reads as a few uneven masses, not one even dome.
- **Long shoots and short shoots set the crown edge.** In a vigorous tree the leader and some side shoots at the top are long shoots, making a "network structure" that extends the crown. - **What distress looks like.** In an ancient tree the outer crown shrinks episodically, and new epicormic shoots grow in the mid and lower crown. Old trees survive through epicormic growth, adventitious rooting, layering and suckering. *My inference:* a crown whose every limb is covered in straight upright shoots reads as a tree reacting to heavy damage or cutting. A healthy mature crown edge is a fine net of long shoots.

## 2. How branches taper and join

- **The branch-area rule.** A mother branch of diameter *d* splitting into daughters *dᵢ* obeys *d*^Δ = Σ *dᵢ*^Δ on average. Measured Δ is between 1.8 and 2.3 for many species (Δ = 2 means cross-sectional area is conserved). *Arithmetic from the rule:* with Δ = 2, two equal daughters are each about 0.71 of the mother's diameter. A daughter with a quarter of the area has half the diameter, and the mother continuing past it drops only to about 0.87 of its former diameter.
- **Why: two explanations.** The *pipe model* (Shinozaki et al. 1964) pictures a tree as a bundle of unit pipes, each connecting a set of leaves to the roots. So the stem area at a height tracks the leaves above it. Below the crown, the pipes of branches long since shed stay in the trunk as "disused pipes." That is why trunks keep thickening toward the base even where no branches remain. Eloy objects that the conducting sapwood can be as little as 5% of a mature trunk's cross-section. He shows instead that the rule follows if a self-similar tree skeleton sizes its diameters to resist wind. Whatever the cause, cross-sections sum roughly at forks.
- **When the rule bends.** Models depart from the rule as side branches get heavier or leave at wider angles. In real branches the departure is small. Beech branches fit a constant-stress design best; fir branches often follow the area rule. *My inference:* a heavy, near-horizontal limb is somewhat thicker at its base than the area rule alone would give.
- **What a junction is.** The cambium runs continuously from trunk to branch. In the upper junction, though, its cells are oriented at "approximately right angles" to the normal direction. Early in the season the branch xylem turns downward at the branch base and "encircles it to form a collar." Later in the season a collar of trunk xylem envelops it. "The branch is structurally attached to the trunk by a series of trunk collars that envelop the branch collars every growing season." Water enters and leaves the branch through the branch collar. Outwardly there is a branch collar on the underside of the branch base and a branch bark ridge on top, running roughly parallel to the branch angle.
- **Why a side branch never starts thinner than it is farther out.** *My inference, from and:* at its base a branch carries the pipes for every leaf beyond it, and each year's collar adds wood there first. Its cross-section therefore shrinks outward, stepwise at each fork and gradually between forks, and never the other way. A branch drawn as a constant-width rod, or narrower where it leaves the trunk, contradicts both.
- **Angle of attachment.** Wide, U-shaped unions are strong. Narrow V-shaped unions "often form included bark," a wedge of inward-rolled bark between two stems. Codominant stems of about equal size from one point often do the same. When a leader is damaged, several branches may become codominant.
- **Dead branches and stubs.** Around a dead branch, the collar and branch bark ridge "continue to grow" and can be told apart from the dead wood. *General knowledge:* over years a living collar can form a sleeve around a dead stub.

### Whites

  paint film, and dries rapidly"; lead white is a rapid dryer. Period tube paints held "linseed oil in the darker colours and

  break fell from 7.3% at 0.2 years to under 1%. Lead-soap
  protrusions can form in a lead-white ground.
- **zinc white** (zinc oxide). In oil it "tends … to form hard, often
  brittle films" that crack over softer layers. Aged zinc white

local function line(knots, step, amp, nseed)
  local n = noise{seed=nseed, octaves=4, period=45}
  local out = {}

    local a, b = knots[i], knots[i+1]
    local steps = math.max(1, math.floor((b[1]-a[1]) / step))
    for s = 0, steps - 1 do

      out[#out+1] = {x, y}

I'm setting up a piecewise linear blend between color stops along the y-axis — deep sky at top, through blue, mid, lilac, belt, eshadow, mist_far, down to bright and low mist — using hat functions that sum to one, plus a gaussian glow weight near the moon. local stops = {{0, sky_deep}, {95, sky_blue}, {170, sky_mid}, {218, sky_lilac}, {258, belt}, {305, eshadow}, {345, eshadow}, {400, mist_far}, {478, mist_bright}, {545, mist_bright}, {700, mist_low}}
local function hat(i)
  return function(x, y)
    local c = stops[i][1]
    local lo = stops[i-1] and stops[i-1][1] or -1e9
    local hi = stops[i+1] and stops[i+1][1] or 1e9
    if y <= c then
      if i == 1 then return 1 end
      return math.max(0, (y - lo) / (c - lo))
    else
      if i == #stops then return 1 end
      return math.max(0, (hi - y) / (hi - c))
    end
  end
end
local piles = {}
for i = 1, #stops do piles[#piles+1] = {stops[i][2], hat(i)} end
piles[#piles+1] = {glow, function(x, y) local dx, dy = (x - moonC[1]) / 85, (y - moonC[2]) / 55; return 0.7 * math.exp(-(dx*dx + dy*dy)) end}
ATM = -FGmask

arguments.lua:
function crest_fn(line)
  -- piecewise-linear y at x along a line sorted by x
  local pts = {}
  for _, p in ipairs(line) do pts[#pts+1] = p end
  table.sort(pts, function(a, b) return a[1] < b[1] end)
  return function(x)
    if x <= pts[1][1] then return pts[1][2] end
    if x >= pts[#pts][1] then return pts[#pts][2] end
    local lo, hi = 1, #pts
    while hi - lo > 1 do
      local mid = (lo + hi) // 2
      if pts[mid][1] <= x then lo = mid else hi = mid end
    end
    local a, b = pts[lo], pts[hi]
    local t = (x - a[1]) / math.max(1e-6, b[1] - a[1])
    return a[2] + (b[2] - a[2]) * t
  end
end
-- region below a line down to depth (a function of x), as a polygon
function band_below(line, depth_fn)
  local q = {}
  for _, p in ipairs(line) do q[#q+1] = {p[1], p[2]} end
  for i = #line, 1, -1 do local p = line[i]; q[#q+1] = {p[1], p[2] + depth_fn(p[1])} end
  return poly(q)
end
-- the underlayer's mist piles by y (the same stops as the sky campaign)
SKYSTOPS = {{0, sky_deep}, {95, sky_blue}, {170, sky_mid}, {218, sky_lilac}, {258, belt}, {305, eshadow}, {345, eshadow}, {400, mist_far}, {478, mist_bright}, {545, mist_bright}, {700, mist_low}}
function sky_hat(i)
  local stops = SKYSTOPS
  return function(x, y)
    local c = stops[i][1]
    local lo = stops[i-1] and stops[i-1][1] or -1e9
    local hi = stops[i+1] and stops[i+1][1] or 1e9
    if y <= c then
      if i == 1 then return 1 end
      return math.max(0, (y - lo) / (c - lo))
    else
      if i == #stops then return 1 end
      return math.max(0, (hi - y) / (hi - c))
    end
  end
end
-- graded piles: ridge pile near the crest fading to the underlayer's own colors below
function ridge_piles(rp, cf, d0, fade, extra)
  local wr = function(x, y) return clamp(1 - (y - cf(x) - d0) / fade, 0, 1) end
  local list = {{rp, wr}}
  for i = 6, #SKYSTOPS do
    local h = sky_hat(i)
    list[#list+1] = {SKYSTOPS[i][2], function(x, y) return (1 - wr(x, y)) * h(x, y) end}
  end
  return list
end

function spruce2(s, seed)
  math.randomseed(seed)
  local h = s.base - s.tip
  local parts = {}
  local branches = {}
  -- leader
  parts[#parts+1] = ribbon({{s.x, s.tip}, {s.x + rand(-1,1), s.tip + h * 0.12}}, {0.6, math.max(1.2, s.w * 0.04)})
  parts[#parts+1] = ribbon({{s.x, s.tip + h*0.1}, {s.x, s.base}}, {math.max(1.2, s.w*0.04), math.max(2, s.w * 0.08)})
  local y = s.tip + h * 0.04
  while y < s.base - 4 do
    local t = (y - s.tip) / h
    local env = s.w / 2 * math.min(1, (t ^ 0.8) * 1.05) 
    local sp = clamp(h / 30, 2.2, 16) * (0.6 + 0.8 * math.random())
    for _, side in ipairs({-1, 1}) do
      if math.random() > 0.12 then
        local L = env * (0.45 + 0.7 * math.random())
        local droop = L * (0.25 + 0.3 * math.random())
        local y0 = y + rand(-sp*0.3, sp*0.3)
        local th = clamp(sp * (0.55 + 0.4*math.random()), 1.2, 14)
        local pts = {{s.x, y0}, {s.x + side * L * 0.45, y0 + droop * 0.55}, {s.x + side * L * 0.85, y0 + droop}, {s.x + side * L, y0 + droop * 0.85}}
        parts[#parts+1] = ribbon(pts, {th, th * 0.8, th * 0.55, th * 0.25})
        branches[#branches+1] = {pts=pts, th=th}
        -- pendant clumps under the branch
        local nc = math.floor(L / math.max(3, th * 1.2))
        for k = 1, nc do
          local u = math.random() * 0.9 + 0.1
          local cx = s.x + side * L * u
          local cy = y0 + droop * u + th * (0.3 + 0.4 * math.random())
          parts[#parts+1] = ellipse(cx, cy, th * (0.25 + 0.3 * math.random()), th * (0.35 + 0.4 * math.random()))
        end
      end
    end
    y = y + sp
  end
  local m = parts[1]
  for i = 2, #parts do m = m + parts[i] end
  m = m:roughen(math.max(0.8, s.w * 0.02), math.max(4, s.w * 0.12), seed)
  return m, branches
end
function paint_spruce2(s, pile_, seed, clipm)
  local m, br = spruce2(s, seed)
  if clipm then m = m * clipm end
  work(m, {hand="body", pile=pile_, angle=1.3, coverage=2.5, fill=true, clip=m, tool={kind="filbert", width=clamp(s.w / 12, 1.5, 7)}})
  return m
end

function lip_line(x0, x1, y0, seed, seg, jump, slope)
  math.randomseed(seed)
  local pts = {}
  local x, y = x0, y0
  local n = noise{seed=seed, octaves=3, period=40}
  pts[#pts+1] = {x, y}
  while x < x1 do
    local L = rand(seg[1], seg[2])
    local xe = math.min(x1, x + L)
    local steps = math.max(2, math.floor((xe - x) / 5))
    for s = 1, steps do
      local xx = x + (xe - x) * s / steps
      pts[#pts+1] = {xx, y + (xx - x0) * (slope or 0) + 1.5 * n(xx, y0)}
    end
    x = xe
    if x < x1 then
      local dy = rand(-jump, jump)
      y = y + dy
      x = x + rand(0.5, 2)
      pts[#pts+1] = {x, y + (x - x0) * (slope or 0) + 1.5 * n(x, y0)}
    end
  end
  return pts
end
function between(upper, lower)
  local q = {}
  for _, p in ipairs(upper) do q[#q+1] = p end
  for i = #lower, 1, -1 do q[#q+1] = lower[i] end
  return poly(q)
end
function shifted(line, dy)
  local q = {}
  for _, p in ipairs(line) do q[#q+1] = {p[1], p[2] + dy} end
  return q
end

function lineF(knots, step, amp, nseed)
  local n = noise{seed=nseed, octaves=4, period=45}
  local out = {}
  for i = 1, #knots - 1 do
    local a, b = knots[i], knots[i+1]
    local steps = math.max(1, math.floor(math.abs(b[1]-a[1]) / step))
    for s = 0, steps - 1 do
      local t = s / steps
      local u = t*t*(3-2*t)
      local x = a[1] + (b[1]-a[1]) * t
      local y = a[2] + (b[2]-a[2]) * u + amp * n(x, a[2])
      out[#out+1] = {x, y}
    end
  end
  out[#out+1] = {knots[#knots][1], knots[#knots][2]}
  return out
end

function crest_fn(line)
  local pts = {}
  for _, p in ipairs(line) do pts[#pts+1] = p end
  table.sort(pts, function(a, b) return a[1] < b[1] end)
  return function(x)
    if x <= pts[1][1] then return pts[1][2] end
    if x >= pts[#pts][1] then return pts[#pts][2] end
    local lo, hi = 1, #pts
    while hi - lo > 1 do local mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if pts[mid][1] <= x then lo = mid else hi = mid end end
    local a, b = pts[lo], pts[hi]
    local t = (x - a[1]) / math.max(1e-6, b[1] - a[1])
    return a[2] + (b[2] - a[2]) * t
  end
end

local nb = noise{seed=177, octaves=4, period=110, stretch={0, 4}, warp={80, 25}}
local function depth(x, y) return clamp((y - cFG(x)) / 190, 0, 1) end

local function wdeep(x, y) return depth(x, y) ^ 0.8 * 1.3 end

function facet_rock(cx, by, w, h, seed)
  math.randomseed(seed)
  -- silhouette: a low irregular mound
  local L, R = cx - w/2, cx + w/2
  local apx = cx + rand(-0.2, 0.2) * w
  local pts = {{L, by, "c"}, {L + w*0.05, by - h*0.55}, {L + w*0.2, by - h*0.9, "c"}, {apx, by - h}, {R - w*0.2, by - h*0.85, "c"}, {R - w*0.04, by - h*0.45}, {R, by, "c"}}
  local o = outline{pts=pts, char="broken", seed=seed, closed=true, amount=0.9}
  local B = o:mask()
  -- facets: top region (above a curve at ~45% height), left front, right side split at a ridge from apex down
  local topY = by - h * 0.5
  local ridgeX = apx + w * 0.12
  local top = B * above(lineF({{L-5, topY + h*0.08}, {cx, topY - h*0.05}, {R+5, topY + h*0.12}}, 5, h*0.06, seed+1))
  local side = (B - top) * mask(function(x, y) return x > ridgeX + (y - topY) * 0.25 and 1 or 0 end)
  local front = B - top - side
  work(front, {hand="body", piles={{rock_mid, 1}, {fg_dark, 0.6}}, coverage=3, fill=true, clip=front, angle=1.3, angle_jitter=0.3, tool={kind="filbert", width=4}})
  work(side, {hand="body", piles={{fg_deep, 1}, {fg_dark, 0.4}}, coverage=3, fill=true, clip=side, angle=1.5, angle_jitter=0.3, tool={kind="filbert", width=4}})
  work(top, {hand="body", piles={{rock_top2, 1}, {fg_dark, 0.5}}, coverage=3, fill=true, clip=top, angle=0.1, angle_jitter=0.3, tool={kind="filbert", width=4}})
  blend(B:shrink(1), {angle=0.3, tool={kind="badger", width=10}})
  -- contact shadow at the base
  local cs = ribbon({{L - 4, by + 1}, {cx, by + 2}, {R + 6, by + 1}}, {2, 4, 2})
  work(cs, {hand="detail", pile=fg_deep, coverage=3, fill=true, clip=cs, angle=0, tool={kind="round", width=1.5}})
  return B
end

function crest_fn(line)
  local pts = {}
  for _, p in ipairs(line) do pts[#pts+1] = p end
  table.sort(pts, function(a, b) return a[1] < b[1] end)
  return function(x)
    if x <= pts[1][1] then return pts[1][2] end
    if x >= pts[#pts][1] then return pts[#pts][2] end
    local lo, hi = 1, #pts
    while hi - lo > 1 do local mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if pts[mid][1] <= x then lo = mid else hi = mid end end
    local a, b = pts[lo], pts[hi]
    local t = (x - a[1]) / math.max(1e-6, b[1] - a[1])
    return a[2] + (b[2] - a[2]) * t
  end
end
-- soft lobes: each a rounded shape; its upper part (far, catching the sky) a touch lighter, lower part darker; edges soft
function lobe(cx, cy, rx, ry, seed, light)
  local m = ellipse(cx, cy, rx, ry):roughen(math.max(2, ry * 0.15), math.max(10, rx * 0.4), seed)
  local top = cy - ry
  local wl = function(x, y) return clamp(1 - (y - top) / (ry * 1.4), 0, 1) * (light or 0.6) end

  return m
end

function pine(base, seed, sc)
  math.randomseed(seed)
  local bx, by = base[1], base[2]
  local function P(dx, dy) return {bx + dx * sc, by + dy * sc} end
  -- trunk: leans right, bends back
  local trunk = {P(0, 0), P(3, -30), P(10, -62), P(12, -95), P(8, -122), P(11, -140)}
  local tm = ribbon(trunk, {7*sc, 5.6*sc, 4.6*sc, 3.6*sc, 2.6*sc, 1.4*sc})
  local limbs = {
    {P(10, -62), P(-8, -70), P(-26, -72), P(-38, -78)},
    {P(12, -88), P(28, -96), P(44, -98)},
    {P(11, -105), P(-4, -114), P(-18, -118)},
    {P(9, -122), P(22, -130), P(30, -133)},
    {P(4, -40), P(-10, -46)},
  }
  local lw = {{2.6, 2, 1.4, 0.8}, {2.4, 1.6, 0.7}, {2, 1.4, 0.6}, {1.6, 1.0, 0.5}, {1.8, 0.6}}
  local wood = tm
  for i, l in ipairs(limbs) do
    local ws = {}
    for k, w in ipairs(lw[i]) do ws[k] = w * sc end
    wood = wood + ribbon(l, ws)
  end
  -- foliage pads: flat, ragged clouds at limb ends and along their tops
  local pads = {
    {P(-34, -82), 20, 6.5}, {P(-20, -77), 13, 5}, {P(40, -102), 19, 6}, {P(26, -100), 12, 5},
    {P(-14, -122), 15, 5.5}, {P(-2, -118), 10, 4.5}, {P(26, -137), 13, 5}, {P(12, -146), 10, 5},
    {P(-8, -50), 9, 3.5},
  }
  local fm = nil
  for _, p in ipairs(pads) do
    local e = ellipse(p[1][1], p[1][2], p[2] * sc, p[3] * sc)
    for k = 1, 4 do

    end
    fm = fm and (fm + e) or e
  end
  fm = fm:roughen(1.6 * sc, 5 * sc, seed)
  return wood, fm
end

arguments.lua:
function crest_fn(line)
  local pts = {}
  for _, p in ipairs(line) do pts[#pts+1] = p end
  table.sort(pts, function(a, b) return a[1] < b[1] end)
  return function(x)
    if x <= pts[1][1] then return pts[1][2] end
    if x >= pts[#pts][1] then return pts[#pts][2] end
    local lo, hi = 1, #pts
    while hi - lo > 1 do local mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if pts[mid][1] <= x then lo = mid else hi = mid end end
    local a, b = pts[lo], pts[hi]
    local t = (x - a[1]) / math.max(1e-6, b[1] - a[1])
    return a[2] + (b[2] - a[2]) * t
  end
end
-- a step: lip line; above it a soft lit band; below it a dark riser of varying height; ends fade
function step(knots, seed, riser, litw, clipm)
  local L = lineF(knots, 4, 1.6, seed)
  local cf = crest_fn(L)
  local x0, x1 = knots[1][1], knots[#knots][1]
  local nr = noise{seed=seed + 5, octaves=3, period=30}
  local function endfade(x) return clamp(math.min(x - x0, x1 - x) / 25, 0, 1) end
  local lit = mask(function(x, y)
    if x < x0 or x > x1 then return 0 end
    local d = cf(x) - y
    if d < 0 or d > litw then return 0 end
    return (1 - d / litw) * endfade(x)
  end)
  local ris = mask(function(x, y)
    if x < x0 or x > x1 then return 0 end
    local h = riser * (0.5 + 0.5 * nr(x, 0)) * endfade(x)
    local d = y - cf(x)
    return (d >= 0 and d <= h) and 1 or 0
  end)
  if clipm then lit = lit * clipm; ris = ris * clipm end
  work(lit, {hand="body", pile=fg_top, coverage=2, fill=true, clip=lit, angle=0, load=0.5, tool={kind="filbert", width=3}, length={10, 30}})
  work(ris, {hand="detail", piles={{fg_deep, 1}, {crack_dark, 0.6}}, coverage=3, fill=true, clip=ris, angle=0, tool={kind="round", width=1.5}})
  blend(lit:grow(2):soften(2), {angle=0, tool={kind="badger", width=8}})
end

    local u = rand(-1, 1)

  end
  -- a few lit tips, upper left

    b:gesture({{x0, top + L * 0.8, 0.5}, {x0 + math.cos(a) * L, top + L * 0.8 + math.sin(a) * L, 0.0}})

local face = rect(300, 520, 110, 190)
local nv = noise{seed=4, octaves=3, period=30, stretch={1.5708, 4}}
local cols = {300, 322, 351, 368, 392, 410}
local function colphase(x, y)
  local xx = x + 3 * nv(x, y)
  for i = 1, #cols - 1 do
    if xx >= cols[i] and xx < cols[i+1] then return (xx - cols[i]) / (cols[i+1] - cols[i]) end
  end
  return 0.5
end

Overall this reads as a convincing Friedrich-style composition—figure, mist, moon, receding ridges—but a couple things could be refined: the moon might benefit from a soft halo glow rather than being a flat disk, and the foreground plateau feels like a large flat brown mass taking up too much space.

The left distant mountain reads a bit flat—maybe mist bands across it would help. To push this closer to Friedrich's style, I'm considering darkening the plateau and adding low rock slabs close in value to the ground rather than distinct boulders, since my earlier boulder attempts didn't work; the plateau's simplicity might just need to be accepted instead.

I'm also puzzled by that vertical seam near x≈548 where the plateau meets the cliff face—trying to work out whether this reads correctly as the cliff's corner given the perspective, since the geometry of a vertical edge running down to the bottom implies something about how the near plateau wall should be oriented that doesn't quite add up yet.

Actually, that stepped region could be read two ways: as the plateau's top surface receding into the distance, or as a cliff face seen frontally with ledges — I painted it with vertical strokes and joints, so it leans toward reading as a face, but it's genuinely ambiguous since a cliff that curves toward the viewer could plausibly show this silhouette.

The geometry is a little unusual but not impossible, and most viewers won't scrutinize it this closely — the painting reads fine as a cliff. I could still soften that vertical seam at x=548 with a subtler transition, but it's a minor fix.

For next priorities, I'm thinking about adding a subtle moon halo using a graded glow technique in the sky around it, though the dry sky surface complicates this.

For the plateau, I want hatched heath overlapping the rock edges to integrate them, keeping it a quiet dark mass like Friedrich's rocky foregrounds, though the current olive-brown feels bland while the heath texture itself works. For mist, I should add soft wisps crossing the forested ridge and spruces, and maybe mist rising behind the figure near the brink, echoing the fog in "Wanderer." The big spruces' trunks also need attention since their lower parts fade too pale and streaky.

On the sky, I'm weighing whether to add a faint evening star, but since this is a moonrise scene the figure faces east, so a western evening star doesn't belong—better to skip it or keep it very subtle. I'm pleased that the physics actually works here: a full moon rising at dusk is correct opposite the setting sun, which makes the pink Belt of Venus band above the blue-gray earth shadow scientifically accurate for this exact view, so I just need to nail its placement and width in the sky.

I should test the halo on scratch first since a radial glow can easily look like a bullseye instead of a subtle glow—Friedrich's moons have that soft quality I want to replicate using the same layered sky technique around the moon.

function lineF(knots, step, amp, nseed)
  local n = noise{seed=nseed, octaves=4, period=45}
  local out = {}
  for i = 1, #knots - 1 do
    local a, b = knots[i], knots[i+1]
    local steps = math.max(1, math.floor(math.abs(b[1]-a[1]) / step))
    for s = 0, steps - 1 do
      local t = s / steps
      local u = t*t*(3-2*t)
      local x = a[1] + (b[1]-a[1]) * t
      local y = a[2] + (b[2]-a[2]) * u + amp * n(x, a[2])
      out[#out+1] = {x, y}
    end
  end
  out[#out+1] = {knots[#knots][1], knots[#knots][2]}
  return out
end
-- an outcrop: silhouette, then a soft top lightening driven by distance below the silhouette top (computed per column)
function outcrop(pts, seed, topdepth)
  local o = outline{pts=pts, char="broken", seed=seed, closed=true, amount=0.7}
  local B = o:mask()
  local tops = {}
  for x = 0, 1000, 2 do
    local ty = nil
    for y = 300, 714, 1 do if B:at(x, y) > 0.5 then ty = y; break end end
    tops[#tops+1] = ty or 9999
  end
  local function topy(x) local i = clamp(math.floor(x / 2) + 1, 1, #tops); return tops[i] end
  local nv = noise{seed=seed, octaves=3, period=25, stretch={1.4, 3}}
  local function wc(x, y) return clamp(1 - (y - topy(x)) / topdepth, 0, 1) * 0.85 end
  local function wf(x, y) return (1 - wc(x, y)) * clamp(0.5 + 0.8 * nv(x, y), 0.1, 1) end
  local function wd(x, y) return (1 - wc(x, y)) * clamp(0.5 - 0.8 * nv(x, y), 0, 1) end

  blend(B:shrink(1), {angle=1.2, tool={kind="badger", width=10}})

end

  local piles = {{halo, wh}, {sky_lilac, function(x, y) return ws(x, y) * hat(218, 40)(x, y) end}, {belt, function(x, y) return ws(x, y) * hat(258, 45)(x, y) end}, {eshadow, function(x, y) return ws(x, y) * clamp((y - 258) / 47, 0, 1) end}, {glow, function(x, y) return ws(x, y) * 0.7 * math.exp(-(((x - cx) / 85) ^ 2 + ((y - cy) / 55) ^ 2)) end}}

## Handoff — day 135 (finished for this sitting)
State: all dry. Title: "Moonrise over the Sea of Mist".
What holds: big value structure (dark plateau and cliff on the left, light mist sea, ridges that pale with distance, a deep smalt sky at the top, the rose belt), the Rückenfigur against the mist, the moon, and the receding file of spruces fading into the mist. In gallery light the brushed ground's striations show through the thin sky, which is right for his manner.
Unresolved / could take further:
- The plateau is still a broad, rather uniform olive-brown mass. The heath hatching helps but reads a little 'grass-texture'. Any repoussoir rock I tried there failed (see below).
- The moon has no halo. Two halo methods failed (below).
- There is a faint vertical seam where the plateau meets the cliff face strip (x≈548), and a slightly pale outline along the cliff's step edges.
- The figure's head reads slightly warm/light between cap and collar at full size. Touches with a round 2.0 didn't change it visibly. Cause unclear: maybe pressure, a small load, or the clip.
Practical lessons (hypotheses unless noted):
- Graded `piles` by y with hat weights + broad filbert 22 lay 1.6 cov 3.5 fill + ONE badger-60 pass = smooth sky. Two badger passes lift paint and show the weave (seen twice).
- Lay ridges/forms over the sky only once it is touch-DRY. Wet or setting sky gave milky, blotchy forms (seen on scratch, 2 trials).
- To lose a form's foot in the mist, grade the form's own piles into the mist's original stops over 30–110 units and badger once, clipped to the form. This worked for the ridges, spruces and valley mist (seen many times).
- A rag lift of open paint over a dry underlayer works with 3–5 FRESH rags (dip .95, pressure .9, crossing angles); then restate the underlying mixture and badger. Mask wipes run past the mask: never wipe near a contrasting edge, use path wipes along it.
- Knife scrape (pressure 1) cleanly removes small open marks from a dry passage.
- Perspective noise (Z = 4000/(y−horizon)) for vegetation zones gives receding patches. Fixed-scale noise reads flat.
Recipes that failed (don't retry without changing the cause):
- Medium-rich glazes (medium .75–.8, glaze hand) over dry sky or fg left blotches/streaks; thinner .5 scumbles gave a coarse weave grid; stipple veils left speckles.
- Moon halo laid radially with the sky's own piles over the dry sky gave a hard-edged pale disc. Untested idea: lay the halo during the FIRST wet sky pass.
- Repoussoir boulders/outcrops lighter or warmer than the plateau read as cut-outs. Light-rimmed dark domes looked pasted on. The ledge helper read as a grey lozenge. Stippled skyline bushes looked like blobs.
- Spruce as a regular polygon of tiers looked like an icon; spruce2 (union of irregular branch ribbons + pendant ellipses, roughened) works.

content.text:
**Moonrise over the Sea of Mist**

It's dusk, looking east. A lone wanderer in a greatcoat and flat cap stands with his back to us at the edge of a dark sandstone plateau. He looks out over a valley filled with mist. Ridges rise out of it, paler and more violet the further away they are. A small warm moon has just risen into the blue-grey band above the far hills, with a rose band above it and deep smalt blue at the top of the sky. On the right, a wooded ridge floats on the mist, and a file of slender spruces climbs out of the valley. Their lower trunks dissolve into the fog. A young spruce and a dead snag cling to the stepped cliff below his feet.

I worked in Friedrich's way: a warm knifed ground under a brushed lead-white top layer, a graphite drawing, a lean brown first layer for the foreground, then thin graded layers with long drying waits between them. The brushed ground's striations still show through the sky. Details went in last: the spruces, the heath, the figure.

**Handoff, also in the journal:**
- **Still unresolved:**
  - The plateau is a broad, fairly uniform olive-brown mass, and its heath texture reads a little like generic grass.
  - The moon has no halo.
  - There's a faint seam where the plateau meets the cliff face, and a slightly pale outline along the cliff steps.
  - At full size the figure's head reads a little warm between cap and collar. Dabbing dark paint over it with a small brush didn't visibly change it, and I don't know why.
- **What worked:**
  - Smooth graded skies came from a single pass of graded colours, then one pass with a soft blending brush. A second blending pass lifts paint and shows the weave.
  - Ridges and trees only laid cleanly once the sky was fully dry.
  - To make forms fade into the mist, I blended each one's own colours into the mist colours underneath.
  - Clumsy wet passages came off with several fresh rags dipped in solvent, then I repainted the mist colours underneath.
  - Spacing the heath patches in perspective (closer together near the horizon) made the ground recede.
- **What failed:**
  - Rich transparent glazes and thin pale veils over dry paint left blotches or a coarse weave pattern.
  - A moon halo painted with the sky's own colours over the dry sky left a hard-edged disc, twice. An untested idea is to lay the halo in the first wet sky pass.
  - Every foreground boulder lighter or warmer than the plateau looked like a cut-out, so I lifted them all.
